items.independentDerivation: f(g(x))=sqrt(2x+3), with range y>=0, so its inverse is (x²−3)/2 for x>=0. Separately, f⁻¹(u)=(u²+1)/2 for u>=0; hence f⁻¹(g(x))=((x+2)²+1)/2 for x>=−2. Its endpoint is (−2,1/2), its y-intercept is (0,5/2), and it has no x-intercept. The native graph code includes the complete branch with a continuation arrow and closed endpoint. The inspected source image omits the negative-x portion; the native reconstruction correctly supplies it.
items.reasoningRationale: The hardest demand is distinguishing the inverse of a composite from a composite involving an inverse, then transferring the inverse domain to a sketch. This connects inverse methods, composition and graphical interpretation.

items.reasoningRationale: The student must recognise that inverse cancellation depends on the selected branch and interpret the absolute value for an input outside it. Completing the square and selecting a square-root branch are ordinary prior algebra and inverse-function transfer.

items.independentDerivation: (2y−1)³=8y³−12y²+6y−1. For t=f(x), 2t−1=(2x−1)³, so x=(1+cuberoot(2t−1))/2 and f⁻¹(x)=(1+cuberoot(2x−1))/2. The cubic transformation is one-to-one on the reals. Both source parts are present.
items.reasoningRationale: The explicit expansion and ‘hence’ scaffold direct the student to recognise the transformed cube, then apply the taught inverse procedure and ordinary algebra. The linked steps are routine once the supplied cue is used.
